overview: Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty in 1368 after rebellion against Mongol Yuan rule. Its history includes enormous building projects, skilled workshops and a flourishing world of books and trade. The conventional endpoint, 1644, marks the loss of Beijing; Ming loyalist courts continued afterward. Imported borders are coarse snapshots: the later northeastern outline is especially broad and must not be read as proof of uniform direct administration everywhere inside it.

periods.title: Ming rule before the fall of Beijing
periods.summary: The main dynastic period; later loyalist regimes and the Qing conquest require a separate, longer transition.

items.text: The Forbidden City in Beijing was constructed between 1406 and 1420 for the Yongle emperor, Zhu Di. Its halls, courtyards and gates organised the business and ceremonies of the imperial court. Later Qing rulers also used the complex, and repairs changed it over time. A palace visitor today sees many layers of history beyond its original Ming construction.

Ming builders added substantial masonry defences to a much older history of frontier walls. The Great Wall was a system of towers, shelters, forts and passes as well as long stretches of wall. Routes along it allowed movement between defensive positions. Its immense construction required sustained work and maintenance; it was never simply one wall completed by one emperor.

Between 1405 and 1433, seven imperial maritime expeditions associated with Zheng He travelled through established Indian Ocean networks. The fleets visited Southeast Asia and India, with missions reaching the Persian Gulf and East Africa. They carried diplomacy, goods and demonstrations of imperial power. Sailors were entering busy trading worlds whose merchants had connected these coasts long before.

A blue-and-white porcelain canteen made at Jingdezhen around 1402 to 1424 borrowed its shape from Islamic metal vessels. Its blue decoration came from cobalt. Although shaped like something carried on a shoulder strap, this surviving example seems too heavy for practical use. Smithsonian curators suggest it was ornamental: a water-carrier shape that may have stayed comfortably at home.

Ming paper money pictured what it was worth: a one-guan note showed a string of 1,000 copper coins. Notes were first issued in 1375, although paper currency already had a long Chinese history. The system faced counterfeiting and other problems, while silver increasingly served as money by weight. Carrying a picture of coins was easier than carrying all the coins themselves.

A copper-alloy ritual cup dated 1520 names a county magistrate and academy instructors. Its inscription ends “大明正德庚辰年造”: “Made in the gengchen year of the Zhengde reign of the Great Ming”, equivalent to 1520. The museum transcribes the Chinese in standard script. This surviving object connects writing, local officials and an academy’s ceremonial life; it is not an ordinary pupil’s drinking cup.

The painting Bird peddler, from the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century, shows six boys fascinated by birds, crickets and two white rabbits. Cages, perches and feeding dishes fill the display. The museum identifies this as an idealised aristocratic scene, with a servant playing the seller. It records an elite fantasy of happy childhood, complete with a very tempting pet shop.

At Hongcun in Anhui, a channel dug around 1405 brought water from a nearby stream into the village. Roughly two centuries later, the South Lake enlarged the system. Watercourses linked houses and ponds, and streets followed their course. Planning a neighbourhood meant thinking about where water would flow, alongside where people would walk and build.

Nearby Xidi grew as members of the Hu family developed merchant careers from the fifteenth century. Surviving houses, built and altered across the Ming and Qing periods, commonly combine timber frames, brick walls and a courtyard. Small outer windows helped with security. Wealth from business could return home as buildings, bridges and spaces used by extended families.

sections.title: Books and the study of nature

items.text: Late Ming readers could buy illustrated drama, poetry and art books. The Huntington’s exhibition includes a 1617 edition of The Peony Pavilion with woodblock pictures carved by members of the Huang family. Such publications required collaboration between writers, artists, carvers, printers and publishers. A printed picture was the product of skilled hands as well as a good story.

The Yongle Encyclopedia, compiled from 1403 to 1408, gathered material on subjects ranging from history and geography to religion and science. It was a manuscript compilation, not a printed set for every household. Surviving volumes come from a later copy made in 1562 to 1567. Some preserve passages from earlier books that have since disappeared, making the encyclopedia a refuge for otherwise lost knowledge.

Li Shizhen spent decades assembling the Compendium of Materia Medica; its first draft was completed in 1578. It described plants, animals and minerals thought to have medicinal properties, while revisiting earlier accounts and correcting mistakes. The book records a major effort to organise knowledge about nature and healing. Its historical importance does not establish that every remedy it contains is effective.

ending.text: Li Zicheng’s rebels captured Beijing in April 1644, and the Chongzhen emperor died by suicide. Qing forces entered the city in June after defeating Li with allied troops. Ming loyalist governments then resisted in southern China for years. Thus 1644 marks the loss of the main Ming court, not an overnight replacement of every government, community or cultural tradition.
